statement: My work begins with observation and the passage of time. Through photography and deliberate placement of wooden sticks, stones, and soil, I developed a scene that is grounded and contemplative. Three sticks rise from the earth against a scenic backdrop, each one standing in for an act in the long arc of growing up. The form explores transformation and the quiet accumulation of experience, interacting with space by borrowing from the landscape rather than competing with it. Across this project I became interested in how the simplest natural materials can carry the weight of an entire life's narrative when arranged with care. The relationship between nature and personal becoming is something worth sitting with.

reflection: There is something quietly honest about calling a piece "Hanging by the Edge." I have always lived in that precarious last moment before things are due, chasing the strange electricity that urgency seems to generate in me. But this sculpture forced me to sit with a question I usually avoid: what do I lose by never arriving early enough to truly explore?

I wanted the work to represent something real about myself, so I shaped a human figure from copper wire. Copper felt right because of how willingly it bends, how it almost meets you halfway when you're trying to coax something recognizable out of raw material. The coiling was both instinctive and deliberate. Coils are among my favorite structures to observe, the way they fold energy into themselves, and wrapping the body in them felt like an accurate portrait of that tense, wound-up state I inhabit when I am teetering at the edge of a deadline. The head, a dense tangle of loops, became something like a self portrait of my thoughts, restless and circular and never quite settling. Working in wire taught me that structure and vulnerability are not opposites. Sometimes the most honest form is also the most open one.
statement: My work begins with self-awareness and the strange electricity of doing things at the last possible moment. Through coiling and bending copper wire, I developed a sculptural figure that is open and vulnerable. The human form stands wound tight, its tangled head a portrait of thoughts that circle without settling. This piece explores urgency and the tension between excitement and loss, interacting with space by drawing lines into air rather than building solid mass. I became interested in the honest question this sculpture forced me to confront, what do I miss by never arriving early enough to truly explore? The relationship between structure and vulnerability is what holds this figure upright, both literally and as an idea.

reflection: There is something deeply wonderful about building something with your own hands that connects you to a person who shaped how you saw the world. This project began not with a design concept or an artistic theory but with a feeling. It began with Technoblade, the Minecraft YouTuber whose kindness, humor, and fighting spirit inspired an entire generation of young viewers, myself included. Watching him as a kid felt like being part of something bigger. His iconic crown became a symbol of resilience and joy, and recreating it as a wearable sculpture felt like the most natural and heartfelt direction I could take.

The crown was constructed from a smaller cardboard box that served as the base structure. Because this is a Minecraft inspired piece, the shape is deliberately rectangular, honoring the blocky aesthetic that made that world so recognizable and beloved. The straight edges and flat planes are not a limitation but a defining feature. They carry meaning. They point back to a digital universe that felt like home for so many of us growing up.

For decoration I used ballot box paper, which gave the surface a smooth and almost regal texture. The paper wraps around the cardboard in layered sections, and additional pieces of ballot box paper were cut and arranged to add visual variety and detail across the crown. Two wires were incorporated into the design to give the piece a touch of class, rising from the top and adding a sense of height and elegance. They catch the light in a way that makes the whole sculpture feel a little more alive.

To ensure the crown could actually be worn without falling apart, I reinforced the interior with strips of Shin Ramen cardboard. The ramen box cardboard is surprisingly sturdy, and wrapping it around the inside of the crown gave the structure the strength it needed to sit comfortably on my head. There is something playful about the idea that a piece of food packaging is quietly holding the whole thing together.

Looking back honestly, I think I could have pushed this piece further if I had spent more time hunting for better recyclable materials. The materials I found worked and they gave the crown its own scrappy charm, but with a wider search I could have discovered textures and surfaces that elevated the whole piece even more. That said, working within those constraints taught me something valuable about resourcefulness and making the most of what is in front of you.

I am still missing a photograph of myself wearing the crown, which I plan to take soon against a clean background as required. But even without that image yet, the crown stands on its own as something I am genuinely proud of. It falls under the category of extension, as it sits on top of the body and amplifies presence and identity. Wearing it changes how I carry myself and how others perceive me.

More than anything, this crown is a relic from my childhood. It is a physical reminder of the happiness that Technoblade brought into my life and the lives of so many others. Making it wearable again was not just an assignment. It was a chance to revisit something meaningful and carry it forward. The process of building it filled me with the same excitement I felt as a kid watching those videos, and that is exactly the kind of energy I wanted this sculpture to hold.
statement: My work begins with nostalgia and the warmth of childhood imagination. Through cardboard construction and paper lamination, I developed a wearable sculpture that is playful and deeply personal. Inspired by Technoblade's iconic Minecraft crown, the rectangular form carries the memory of watching someone kind and inspirational during my younger years. This piece explores celebration and remembrance, interacting with space by sitting on the body and transforming the wearer into something from a world that genuinely mattered to them. I became interested in how building a relic from ramen cardboard and ballot box paper can bring a feeling back to life. The relationship between play and sincerity is what makes this crown feel real.

reflection: The three objects I chose are a book, a pen, and a mirror. The book is one I keep on my desk, a constant companion through coursework and curiosity alike. The pen is ordinary, the kind I reach for without thinking when I need to write something down. The mirror is small and personal, something I have looked into more times than I can count.

I chose these objects as a self-portrait because a literal image of myself would only show what is visible on the surface. These three objects reveal something truer about how I move through the world and what I struggle with internally. A photograph of my face cannot capture the tension between who I am and who I am trying to become.

The book represents what matters most to me. I love to listen to others and to absorb information at any cost, to keep taking things in all the time and to learn something new every day. It speaks to a deep cultural value I hold around knowledge and growth, the idea that we are shaped by what we allow into our minds. The pen represents what I aspire to do with all of this input. I want to streamline the information I take in through different sources into crystal clear narrowed down writable thoughts and actions, so that they do not clutter my mind unnecessarily and are not just randomly available in my head. The pen is discipline, the act of making sense out of noise. The mirror represents my weakness. It stands for self-obsession and self-centeredness, the tendency that pulls me back and makes me take lacklustre decisions where I isolate myself unnecessarily. I want to get out of the self-made images of myself that I create and that I think I continuously project around people.

In the arrangement, both the pen and the mirror stand on top of the book, and the pen is positioned looking into the mirror. Each of these objects is interconnected in a deep inexplicable way, continuously competing for my attention. The book serves as the foundation, the base upon which everything else rests, because without the constant intake of information and listening to others, neither reflection nor refinement would have any material to work with. The pen looks into the mirror judging itself before it refines what it has come up with. This captures the tension I live with daily. Before I can distill my thoughts into something clear and actionable, I find myself caught in self-scrutiny, questioning whether what I am about to put down is good enough or true enough. The mirror tempts the pen into hesitation. And yet they all need each other. The book feeds the pen, the mirror forces the pen to confront itself, and the pen ultimately must move past that reflection to create something real. What I hope for is that the pen learns to glance at the mirror without getting trapped in it, to use that moment of self-awareness as a tool for clarity rather than a reason to stop writing altogether.
statement: My work begins with personal inventory and the courage of looking inward without flinching. Through careful arrangement and photography, I developed a still life that is intimate and deliberately symbolic. A book, a pen, and a mirror sit together, each one standing in for something I wanted to examine about myself. This piece explores identity and projection, interacting with space by asking the viewer to read objects as quiet confessions. I became interested in how the mirror complicates everything, representing a tendency toward self-obsession that I want to move past. The relationship between what we absorb from the world and what we project back onto it is what this piece keeps asking me to think about.

reflection: The tool I chose for this project was a comb, something so ordinary that it barely registers as significant in the flow of a day. And yet, for me, it carries a quiet weight that I had not fully articulated until this assignment asked me to slow down and look at it differently.

The comb is part of a small ritual I perform each morning just before I leave for class. There is something deliberate about it. I pick it up, run it through my hair, and in doing so I feel myself settle. It is a moment of focus and concentration, a way of grounding myself before stepping into the demands of the day ahead. It sounds almost too simple to matter, but that brief, repetitive act functions as a kind of threshold between rest and readiness. I am not just fixing my appearance. I am leveling myself.

When I began building the impression using toilet paper rolls and layers of tissue, I was immediately confronted with how deceptively complex the comb's form actually is. It is extremely thin, with closely spaced teeth that run along almost its entire length. Capturing that with tissue required patience and a lot of material. The toilet paper gave the final shell a rough, almost fibrous texture, which contrasted interestingly with how smooth and utilitarian the original comb feels in hand. The thinness of the comb meant the tissue had to be applied carefully to avoid losing the shape altogether. What emerged was a structure that felt simultaneously fragile and strangely sturdy, tethered together by all those layers building on one another.

The impression process made me aware of how much surface area a comb actually has and how all of that surface exists in service of one narrow, repetitive motion. It also made the ritual feel more visible, more real, as though the object had finally earned the significance I had always quietly given it.
statement: My work begins with routine and the unspoken reverence we assign to everyday objects. Through paper lamination and layered tissue, I developed a sculptural impression that is fragile yet surprisingly sturdy. A comb, something so ordinary it barely registers, emerged from dozens of patient layers of toilet paper that captured every tooth and ridge of its deceptively complex surface. This piece explores ritual and embodied knowledge, interacting with space by making a private morning habit visible and tangible. I became interested in how much meaning lives inside repetition, how combing my hair each morning before class is less about appearance and more about grounding myself before stepping into the day. The relationship between routine and identity feels endlessly worth exploring.

reflection: The bag I chose as my container is the first thing I received at UC Santa Cruz on my orientation day. It is not a neutral object. It came loaded with the promise of a new beginning, handed to me by an institution welcoming me into a place I did not yet know how to inhabit.

Using it as the foundation of this assemblage felt necessary precisely because of that tension between what the bag was supposed to represent and what my actual experience of that time looked and felt like.

Inside the bag I placed a watch that belongs to my father. I took it from him in high school, and carrying it into this new chapter of my life was something I did without fully understanding why. For this piece, the watch represents lost time, a strange sleepwalking quality that defined much of my first period at Santa Cruz. I was present physically but not truly internalizing what was happening around me. I was moving through days without absorbing them, too disoriented or perhaps too afraid to let experiences land. The watch, hidden inside the bag rather than displayed on the surface, captures that quality of time that was passing without being felt. It is there, it is real, but you have to look for it.

The wheel I included speaks to the constant movement that has characterized my life. Even when I felt lost or frozen internally, things kept moving forward. The wheel does not ask permission to turn. It was important to me that this object exist in relationship to the watch because together they describe something true about that period, time moving, life moving, and me somewhat detached from both.
The headphones represent music and the particular kind of isolation that music can offer.

When I arrived somewhere new and unfamiliar, music became a private world I could return to. It was comfort that did not require explanation or social navigation. Writing served a similar function. The ideas and thoughts I was constantly sitting with had nowhere else to go, and so they went onto the page. Including a reference to writing in the assemblage felt important because it is how I processed what I could not yet speak out loud.

Joseph Cornell's approach to assemblage influenced this work most directly. Cornell built boxes that held objects not for their decorative value but for their psychological weight, their capacity to suggest longing, displacement, and private emotional worlds. That is what I was reaching for.

The bag functions conceptually as both exterior and interior self. On the outside it is an institutional welcome, a clean start. On the inside it holds the quieter and more complicated truth of what that start actually felt like. The arrangement moves from surface to depth deliberately, asking the viewer to look past the obvious gesture of arrival and into something more unresolved and honest.
